question.text: Under the same load, wire A having length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> and cross section <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> stretches uniformly by the same amount as another wire <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math> of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>6</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> and a cross section of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> stretches. The ratio of the Young's modulus of wire <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math> to that of wire <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math> will be:

solution.text:
Elongation in uniform wire under load is given by, Δl=FlSY, where S is area of cross-section.

As F is same for both wire and Δl is also same, we can write

ΔlF=lSY⇒lASAYA=lBSBYB

⇒52.5×10-5×YA=63×10-5×YB

⇒YAYB=1
